name: Kon-Tiki
description: Aged rum with orange curaçao, lemon and orgeat over crushed ice — a Trader Vic build named for Heyerdahl's raft.
funFact: Thor Heyerdahl's balsa raft crossed 4,300 miles of Pacific in 1947; the name was attached to restaurants, drinks and a whole aesthetic within a decade.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a lemon wheel

name: Mariner's Grog
description: Three rums with grapefruit, honey and cinnamon. Grog in the naval sense — rum, water, citrus and something to stop scurvy.
funFact: The Royal Navy issued grog — rum cut with water and citrus — from 1740 until 1970, and the last daily ration was poured on 31 July, still called Black Tot Day.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Outrigger
description: Light rum with passionfruit, lime and a float of dark rum — named for the canoe hull that made Pacific voyaging possible.
funFact: The outrigger float is what let Polynesian voyagers sail thousands of miles of open ocean in canoes; it is the single most consequential piece of Pacific technology.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: A dark rum float and a lime wheel

name: Pi Yi
description: Rum, passionfruit and lime blended and served in a hollowed pineapple. Beachcomber's fruit-vessel showpiece.
funFact: Serving in the hollowed fruit was practical marketing: the vessel cost nothing, could not be stolen easily, and photographed better than any glass.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Served in a hollowed pineapple with a mint sprig

name: Port au Prince
description: Haitian rum with pineapple, lime, falernum and grenadine — one of the few tiki drinks that names its rum's actual origin.
funFact: Haitian rhum is distilled from cane juice rather than molasses, which is why it tastes grassy and vegetal where Jamaican rum tastes of treacle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Tortuga
description: Two rums with orange, lime and a sweet vermouth backbone — unusual for tiki, which almost never uses vermouth.
funFact: Tortuga, off northern Haiti, was the buccaneers' base in the seventeenth century — the actual pirate island the tiki aesthetic was borrowing from.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.

name: Tropical Itch
description: Bourbon and two rums with passionfruit, served with a backscratcher in the glass. The garnish is not optional.
funFact: The bamboo backscratcher is the drink — Hawaiian bars have served it that way since the 1950s, and ordering one without is considered a failure of nerve.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: A bamboo backscratcher and an orchid

name: Coconut Grog
description: Rum with coconut cream, honey, cinnamon and citrus — a grog that went through the tropics rather than the North Atlantic.
funFact: Beachcomber layered spice syrups the way a perfumer layers base notes — cinnamon, vanilla and allspice recur across dozens of his recipes in different proportions.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Toasted coconut and a cinnamon stick

name: Demerara Dry Float
description: A short rum sour under a float of overproof Demerara. The float is the drink's whole architecture.
funFact: A float sits on top because it is less dense; you get the overproof rum on the nose and the first sip, then the drink beneath softens as it mixes.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed ice.
Shake hard for about 10 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug and top with fresh crushed ice.
Garnish generously and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: An overproof float and a lime wheel

name: Japanese Cocktail
description: Cognac, orgeat and bitters. No Japanese ingredient at all — named for a diplomatic delegation that visited New York in 1860.
funFact: Jerry Thomas named it for the first Japanese embassy to the United States, which arrived in 1860 and was received with enormous public curiosity.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Brandy Smash
description: Brandy, sugar and mint pounded over crushed ice. Jerry Thomas called the smash a julep on a small plan, and meant it literally.
funFact: The 1862 Bar-Tender's Guide is the first cocktail book published anywhere, and the smash is one of the six families it organises everything around.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in the bottom of a rocks glass.
Add the brandy and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Top with more crushed ice and crown with a mint bouquet.

name: Gin Sling
description: Gin, lemon, sugar and water, with nutmeg over the top. The sling predates the cocktail and was originally served hot.
funFact: A sling in the eighteenth century was spirit, water, sugar and nutmeg — the cocktail was defined in 1806 specifically as a sling with bitters added.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice, syrup and water with ice.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface.
Serve with a straw.

name: Locomotive
description: Hot red wine with honey, egg yolk and curaçao, whisked smooth. A Victorian hot drink with a custard's texture.
funFact: Nineteenth-century bar books are full of hot egg drinks; central heating and refrigeration between them killed off almost the entire category.

steps: Whisk the egg yolk with the honey until pale and smooth.
Warm the wine with the cloves until steaming — never boiling.
Pour the hot wine slowly onto the egg mixture while whisking hard.
Return briefly to low heat to thicken, then stir in the curaçao.
Serve hot with cinnamon grated over.

name: Golden Slipper
description: Yellow Chartreuse, apricot brandy and an egg yolk floated whole between them. A Victorian layered drink that takes a steady hand.
funFact: The unbroken yolk suspended between two liqueurs is the point — layered pousse-café drinks were a display of bartending skill as much as anything to drink.

steps: Pour the yellow Chartreuse into a small wine glass.
Float the apricot brandy over the back of a barspoon so it layers cleanly.
Slide a whole unbroken egg yolk gently into the centre.
Serve immediately, without stirring.

name: Bishop
description: Port mulled with a clove-studded roasted orange and sugar. The parent of the Smoking Bishop and older than it.
funFact: The whole family is named for ecclesiastical ranks by strength and ingredient — Bishop is port, Cardinal is claret, Pope is champagne, Archbishop is claret with ginger.

steps: Stud an orange with cloves and roast at 180°C until browned, about 45 minutes.
Quarter the roasted orange and add it to the port with the sugar and cinnamon.
Heat gently to steaming for 20 minutes; do not boil.
Strain into warmed mugs and serve hot.

name: Arrack Punch
description: Batavia arrack with lemon, sugar, tea and water. The original punch, brought back from the Indies by the East India Company.
funFact: Punch reached England from India in the seventeenth century and the word probably comes from panch, Hindi for five — spirit, citrus, sugar, water and spice.

steps: Rub the sugar into the lemon peel and leave for an hour to draw out the oil.
Add the lemon juice and stir until the sugar dissolves, then strain out the peel.
Add the arrack and the hot tea, and stir well.
Chill thoroughly, or serve warm in winter.
Ladle into cups over a block of ice, with nutmeg grated on top.

name: Cambridge Milk Punch
description: Brandy and rum in hot milk with sugar, lemon and egg, whisked to a froth. A university drink from before the cocktail existed.
funFact: Distinct from clarified milk punch, where the milk is curdled and strained out — here the milk stays in, and the drink is served hot and foaming.

steps: Warm the milk with the lemon peel and sugar until steaming, then discard the peel.
Beat the egg hard in a separate bowl.
Pour the hot milk slowly onto the egg while whisking, or it will scramble.
Stir in the brandy and rum off the heat and whisk until foaming.
Serve hot with nutmeg grated over.

name: Regent's Punch
description: Champagne, brandy, rum, arrack and tea over citrus — the Prince Regent's punch, and about as extravagant as it sounds.
funFact: Named for the future George IV, whose household spent so freely on entertaining that Parliament twice had to settle his debts.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the cooled tea and citrus juice.
Add the brandy, rum and arrack and stir well.
Chill for several hours with a large block of ice in the bowl.
Top with champagne only at the moment of serving.
Ladle into cups, giving each a wheel of citrus.
recipe.garnish: Citrus wheels and a block of ice

name: Stone Wall
description: Aged rum over hard cider with bitters. Colonial New England drank it before the word cocktail was written down.
funFact: New England distilled rum from Caribbean molasses and pressed cider from its own orchards, so a drink combining the two was the cheapest thing on the table.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum and the bitters.
Top with cold hard cider.
Stir once and garnish with an apple slice.

name: Green Beast
description: Absinthe, lime, sugar and water with cucumber — a low-proof absinthe punch that converts people who think they hate absinthe.
funFact: Charles Vexenat built it as equal parts absinthe, lime, sugar and water — the classic punch ratio — which dilutes absinthe to about the strength of wine.

steps: Combine the absinthe, lime juice and syrup in a tall glass.
Add the cold water and stir — it will louche to opaque green.
Fill with ice and stir again briefly.
Float cucumber wheels on the surface and serve.

name: Newark
description: Applejack, sweet vermouth, Fernet and maraschino — a Brooklyn built on apple brandy, and named across the river.
funFact: Jim Meehan and Toby Maloney built it as a Brooklyn variation; Laird's in New Jersey has been distilling applejack since 1780 and holds America's oldest distilling licence.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Marconi Wireless
description: Applejack and sweet vermouth with orange bitters — a Manhattan made with apple brandy, named for the radio.
funFact: Marconi sent the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901, and American bars named drinks after the technology the way they later would after aviation.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Rattlesnake
description: Rye, lemon, sugar and egg white with an absinthe rinse. The Savoy says it will 'either cure a rattlesnake bite, kill rattlesnakes, or make you see them'.
funFact: That three-part claim is printed verbatim in the Savoy Cocktail Book, which is unusually candid for a drinks list of any era.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Dry-shake the rye, lemon, syrup and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into the rinsed coupe and let the foam settle.

name: Tia Mia
description: A Mai Tai split between mezcal and Jamaican rum. Smoke where the second rum was, and it changes the whole drink.
funFact: Ivy Mix created it at Leyenda in Brooklyn; the name is an anagram of Mai Tai, which is also exactly what the drink is.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig and the spent lime shell.
Serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Mint sprig and a spent lime shell

name: Chrysanthemum Royale
description: The Chrysanthemum lengthened with champagne — vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe under bubbles.
funFact: Adding champagne to an existing cocktail and calling it 'Royale' is a French convention that produced the Kir Royale, the French 75 and a dozen lesser drinks.

steps: Stir the vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express an orange twist over the surface and serve.

name: Bitter Elder
description: Elderflower, Campari and grapefruit over soda. Bitter and floral at once, and low enough proof for an afternoon.
funFact: Elderflower and Campari share a register that most bartenders miss — both are simultaneously perfumed and bitter, which is why they layer rather than fight.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the St-Germain, Campari and grapefruit juice and stir.
Top with soda water and stir once more.
Express a grapefruit twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Chartreuse Daisy
description: Green Chartreuse with lemon, grenadine and soda over crushed ice. A daisy built on a liqueur rather than a spirit.
funFact: The daisy is spirit, citrus and a sweetener topped with soda; swapping the base spirit for Chartreuse is the kind of substitution nineteenth-century books made freely.

steps: Shake the Chartreuse, lemon juice and grenadine with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a mint sprig.

name: Bensonhurst Fizz
description: The Bensonhurst lengthened with soda over ice — rye, dry vermouth, maraschino and Cynar made long.
funFact: Lengthening a stirred drink with soda is the simplest way to make a spirit-forward recipe drinkable in summer, and Brooklyn bars did it to most of the neighbourhood series.

steps: Stir the rye, vermouth, maraschino and Cynar over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water and stir once.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Oaxaca Sour
description: Mezcal, lime and agave under an egg-white foam with a chilli-salt dusting. A smoky sour with heat on the finish.
funFact: Sal de gusano — salt ground with toasted agave worm and chilli — is the traditional Oaxacan accompaniment to mezcal, and works as a dusting where a rim would be too much.

steps: Dry-shake the mezcal, lime, agave and egg white without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust the foam lightly with chilli salt and serve.
